title: I like tea
goal: Say what you like, dislike, and prefer; ask for something politely with *ba mhaith liom*.
bekal: use *Is maith liom / Ní maith liom / An maith leat?* correctly
learn the seven forms of *le*: liom, leat, leis, léi, linn, libh, leo
ask for and offer things with *Ba mhaith liom* and *Ar mhaith leat?*

dialogs.title: Comhrá — Cupán tae
dialogs.intro: After class, Aoife drops by the house and Budi makes tea. The talk turns to likes and dislikes.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: An maith leat an ceol traidisiúnta?
lines.literal: question good with-you the music traditional?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Is breá liom é! Ach ní maith liom an ceol tíre.
lines.id: I love it! But I don't like country music.
lines.literal: is fine with-me it! but not good with-me the music country-of.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Is fearr liom féin an ceol nua-aimseartha.
lines.literal: is better with-me myself the music new-time-of.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Cad faoi bhia? An maith leat bia Indinéiseach?
lines.id: What about food? Do you like Indonesian food?
lines.literal: what about food? question good with-you food Indonesia-of?

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Ní maith liom bia an-te, ach is maith liom rís.
lines.id: I don't like very spicy food, but I like rice.
lines.literal: not good with-me food very-hot, but is good with-me rice.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tá bia na hIndinéise an-te go minic!
lines.id: Indonesian food is often really spicy!
lines.literal: is food the Indonesia-of very-hot often!

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Mar sin, is fearr liom bia na hÉireann. Prátaí!
lines.id: Then I prefer Irish food. Potatoes!
lines.literal: like that, is better with-me food the Ireland-of. potatoes!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Is maith liom prátaí freisin. Ar mhaith leat cupán tae?
lines.id: I like potatoes too. Would you like a cup of tea?
lines.literal: is good with-me potatoes too. question-would good with-you cup tea?

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Ba mhaith, go raibh maith agat. Le bainne, le do thoil.
lines.literal: would good, may-be good at-you. with milk, with your will.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.id: I don't mind. A little, maybe.
lines.literal: is same with-me. a little, maybe.

notes: **Is maith liom is literally "is good with me".** Irish has no verb "to like". Instead it uses the verb *is* (Unit 6) plus the adjective *maith* ("good") plus the preposition *le* ("with"). So "I like tea" comes out as "is good with me tea" — *Is maith liom tae*. The pattern stays the same whatever you like.

**Le swallows its pronoun, like ag and ar.** Its seven forms: *liom, leat, leis, léi, linn, libh, leo*. Note *leis* ("with him"), the odd one out, and *léi* ("with her"), said LYAY. You now have the three most important prepositions: *ag* for having, *ar* for feelings, *le* for liking.

**Ba mhaith liom is not Is maith liom.** *Is maith liom tae* means "I like tea" — a statement of taste. *Ba mhaith liom tae* means "I'd like tea" — a polite request, just like English *I would like*. Mix them up in a café and you'll sound like you're discussing the philosophy of tea instead of ordering it. The question is *Ar mhaith leat …?* and the answer is *Ba mhaith* or *Níor mhaith*.

**Bia na hIndinéise — the possessive form again.** You saw it in *os comhair na heaglaise* (Unit 3). The second noun goes into the possessive form, and the article changes from *an* to *na*, with *h-* before a vowel: *an Indinéis* → *na hIndinéise*, *Éire* → *na hÉireann*. For now, just learn the forms for the countries you mention often.

blocks.text: *Le* is also used for the ordinary "with": *Tar liom* ("come with me"), *Tá mé ag caint léi* ("I'm talking to her"), *tae le bainne* ("tea with milk"). And it is inside two phrases you've used since Unit 1: *le do thoil* ("please", literally "with your will") and *Cé leis é?* ("whose is it?").

blocks.title: After le + an, the noun gets urú
items: *Le* + *an* merge into *leis an*, and the noun after it gets urú: *leis an mbainne*, *leis an gcaife*, *leis an bhfear*.
For the plural, use *leis na*, with no change: *leis na páistí*, *leis na cairde*.
The same pattern holds for *ag an*, *ar an*, *ón*, *faoin* — they all bring urú. The full set is gathered in Unit 19.

blocks.text: Notice that the answer to *An maith leat …?* is not *Tá* and not *Sea*, but the adjective repeated: *Is maith* or *Ní maith*. It's the "repeat the verb" pattern you've known since Unit 2, used with the verb *is*.

English

I don't like very spicy food.

Say it
English
rows: Ba mhaith liom caife, le do thoil.
Ba mhaith, go raibh maith agat.
Níor mhaith, go raibh maith agat.

blocks.title: Four phrases to take to any café
items: *Ba mhaith liom cupán tae, le do thoil.* — "I'd like a cup of tea, please."
*Cé mhéad atá air?* — "How much is it?"
*Tá sé sin go breá, go raibh maith agat.* — "That's fine, thank you."
*Slán, go raibh míle maith agat.* — "Bye, thanks a lot" (literally "a thousand thanks").

blocks.text: *Ba mhaith* is actually the conditional form of *is maith* — "would be good". English does the same with *would like*: a softer form makes the request more polite. The full conditional comes at A2.
